denoising: At t=0.50, Gaussian blur suppresses noise but loses the puppy’s fur and facial detail. The one-step model reconstructs the eyes and nose while keeping the fur smooth; Euler sampling adds sharper-looking fur texture and a more distinct nose, with some change from the original photograph. The measured source-space MSE is 0.005430 for blur, 0.001504 for one step, and 0.001898 for Euler: the visually sharper Euler output is not the closest reconstruction under pixel MSE. The noisy input, noise realization, and prompt are shared across this comparison.
conditional: All five fixed-seed samples generated with the generic prompt are portraits of people, even though no person is mentioned in the prompt. This small sample therefore shows a strong portrait bias rather than broad subject diversity. Quality varies: seed 180 has an incomplete face, seed 181 has distorted anatomy, and seed 183 has rough, paint-like facial texture. Seeds 182 and 184 have more coherent facial structure. A generic prompt does not by itself ensure a high-quality photograph.
cfg: With identical initial noise seeds, guidance weight 7 produces five much more coherent head-and-shoulders portraits. The missing face at seed 180 and distorted anatomy at seed 181 are resolved, and the rough painterly texture at seed 183 becomes a cleaner photographic face. Guidance changes the subject and composition substantially; it is not simply sharpening the ordinary output. Seed 182 retains a similar hand-near-face pose, but its lighting and features also change. All guided samples remain portraits and have more uniform framing, so this small experiment shows improved visual consistency without increased subject diversity. Some skin and eye details still look overly smooth or stylized.
editing: The Campanile sweep preserves broad color and geometry before fine detail: t=0.02 yields a blurred scene with a smooth white column; t=0.04–0.06 recovers blue sky and trees but invents the top of the structure. At t=0.10–0.14, the tower has a dark rectangular opening instead of the clock and belfry. The recognizable belfry returns at t=0.25, and t=0.50 retains much more of the original clock, stone texture, and surrounding trees. Higher starting time gives stronger source fidelity, though the sampler still modifies fine details.

The puppy is a failure case for the generic prompt. At t=0.02–0.06, the model replaces it with human portraits, echoing the portrait bias in ordinary conditional generation experiments. At t=0.10–0.14, source colors and background structures compete with that interpretation, producing blurred faces. At t=0.25 the puppy-like face has duplicated or distorted muzzle details; t=0.50 recovers a recognizable puppy and its original background but remains soft. More retained source information does not guarantee a clean edit when the prompt prior conflicts with the source.

For the lake, t=0.02 changes the subject entirely into a gray car. At t=0.04–0.06, the original pink-and-blue palette survives as broad abstract bands. At t=0.10–0.14 the model invents a lit shoreline city beneath the sunset. At t=0.25–0.50, the original layered hills, clouds, and water return, although they remain smoother than the source. This sweep shows that colors and coarse layout can survive even when the semantic subject changes.

The downloaded Van Gogh painting changes both subject and style across the sweep. At t=0.02 it becomes a seated human portrait; t=0.04 invents a snowy mountain landscape while retaining the yellow foreground and blue sky. Starting times 0.06–0.14 restore the field-and-cypress layout but produce soft, simplified scenery. At t=0.25 the same layout becomes a photographic-looking field, trees, and clouds. At t=0.50 the original swirling brushwork largely survives. Here an intermediate starting time gives the clearest painting-to-photograph transformation, while the largest time best preserves the source style.

The user hand-drawn sailboat shows the limits of the generic photo prompt with sparse line art. At t=0.02, it becomes a small white rectangular frame or wall fixture; t=0.04–0.06 are almost blank, softly shaded images. At t=0.10 the model produces a pale sheet with horizontal lines, and t=0.14 produces an outlined square panel. Some sail and hull contours return at t=0.25, but they form a distorted, softly shaded object and the waves disappear. At t=0.50, the sailboat and waves are clearly preserved while the screenshot grid is strongly suppressed. This strongest-source result remains a line drawing, so the sweep does not demonstrate a successful conversion into a realistic boat photograph. The complete supplied drawing was retained using square padding before the standard resize.

The user hand-drawn teapot also loses its subject at low starting times: t=0.02 becomes a white rectangular frame, while t=0.04–0.10 are nearly blank pale surfaces. At t=0.14, the model invents faint, unreadable letter-like marks on a square sheet. The teapot outline returns at t=0.25, including its spout and handle, but the lid and lower-right contour are distorted. At t=0.50, the body, lid, spout, and handle are closer to the source and most of the screenshot grid is removed. Neither higher-time output becomes a photographic ceramic teapot. Together with the sailboat, this is evidence that a generic photo prompt and sparse thin strokes can fail to establish the intended object; greater source retention helps preserve recognizable geometry without guaranteeing photorealism.
text_editing: The lighthouse prompt gives much stronger semantic control than the generic photo prompt. At t=0.02–0.04, the result is a clear coastal lighthouse with rocks and blue sky, and the original composition changes substantially. At t=0.06–0.14, the tall source silhouette remains while the belfry becomes a lighthouse lantern or railing and the ground becomes rocky. At t=0.25, the result mixes Campanile windows with lighthouse details; at t=0.50, the Campanile, trees, and stonework dominate again. Thus stronger source retention limits how completely the text can replace the scene.

The dog-specific prompt resolves the generic-prompt portrait failure. At t=0.02–0.06, all outputs show a golden retriever puppy with a bright red knitted scarf in a snowy setting, but identity, pose, and composition differ from the source. At t=0.10–0.14, more of the original dark background returns; one sample turns the puppy sideways, so pose changes are not monotonic. At t=0.25–0.50, the face and indoor-looking background are closer to the source, while the scarf becomes less prominent and snow remains mostly on the fur and foreground. Stronger source preservation competes with the requested environmental change.

The snowy-alpine-lake prompt produces snow-covered mountains, reflective water, and warm dawn light across the low and intermediate starting times. At t=0.02–0.06 it substantially rebuilds the scene into an enclosed alpine valley. At t=0.10–0.25 the mountain band shifts toward the original horizontal composition, while snow and strong reflections remain. At t=0.50 the original layered hills and cloud bands dominate, with a smaller snowy modification. The source sunset palette is compatible with the requested dawn lighting, so it survives even when the landscape geometry changes.
anagrams: The first anagram has two recognizable readings. Upright, dark eye sockets and a central nose frame an old man with a bright white beard. After a 180-degree rotation, the bright beard region becomes firelight and smoke, while the original facial details become people sitting around a campfire. The warm oil-painting style and dark background help both interpretations share the same contours.

The second anagram reads as a mountain village upright, with rooftops beneath steep peaks. Rotated, the rooftops form the horse’s head and the mountain contours become its neck and mane. Both subjects are recognizable, but the low-contrast pencil-like lines make this illusion less immediate at small display sizes than the old-man/campfire example. The paired figure shows exactly the same pixels in the two orientations.
hybrids: The skull/waterfall result is a partial success: falling water, trees, and rocks are clear at full size, but the reduced view mainly retains an oval head-like silhouette. Distinct skull features do not emerge strongly enough, so the intended far-view skull is weak in this seed-180 sample. This limitation is visible in the displayed result.

The forest/cat hybrid has a more convincing scale change. At full size, tree trunks, branches, and ground texture dominate. At the reduced 64-pixel view, those details recede and a cat’s ears, eyes, and muzzle become recognizable. The cat silhouette is still somewhat visible close up, so the separation is imperfect. The result also has a blue/cyan cast despite both prompts requesting black and white.
